#4687. 7 Best At-Home Waxing Kits, Tested by Beauty Experts

Of the 25 wax kits we tested, Flamingo was our favorite.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Body hair is completely normal and natural. But if you’re like me and prefer a hair-free look, then take a page from my beauty editor routine and try at-home waxing kits for dolphin-like skin. Dermatologists told me that at-home waxing kits are a worthwhile hair removal method. Unlike shaving, waxing removes hair at the root, whereas a woman's razor blade simply cuts the hair down, says dermatologist Reshmi Kapoor, MD. It’s a bit painful, but the tenderness quickly disappears and the results are so worth the temporary discomfort. Waxing may lead to finer, sparser regrowth over time, so the skin stays hair-free longer than with shaving, says Dr. Kapoor. My underarms are dramatically smoother, lighter, and have fewer ingrown hairs to boot.

At-home waxing kits prevent unsightly razor bumps and are more cost-effective than replacing dull razors and restocking shaving creams. They're also cheaper than professional waxing sessions and save you time from commuting to the waxing studio.

And sure, applying a glob of wax to your body sounds intimidating, but it's surprisingly easy and not as painful as you'd imagine. In our guide to pain-free waxing, experts revealed some helpful advice, like staying hydrated with water and avoiding alcohol before waxing. Another pro tip: skip waxing a few days before your period because you’re dealing with increased sensitivity. Plus, some at-home waxing kits even contain soothing ingredients like aloe vera that are safe for sensitive skin.

With a low-upkeep routine of every four to six weeks, using at-home waxing kits is a no-brainer beauty move. Ahead, Dr. Kapoor and her fellow dermatologists get real about shopping for at-home waxing kits and share their must-have picks. After ordering our editor-tested, dermatologist-approved recommendations, keep reading for more expert tips on post-waxing care.

Out of all the different at-home waxing kits we tried, these wax strips were the easiest to use and the most effective at picking up every single little hair. Flamingo's wax strips won our top spot because they were super simple to apply with very little prep work besides getting the area clean and dry. The soft wax strips are infused with soothing ingredients, like castor seed oil and beeswax, making them ideal for removing fine hair on larger areas, like your arms. Best of all, they’re ready to go whenever you are—no microwave is required. To use them, simply peel apart the strip and apply it, rubbing firmly against your skin to make sure it coats every hair.

We did find the strips a little too big for areas like the face, but you can always cut them down to the correct size with a pair of scissors. Pulling up the wax strip stung quite a bit for Montemayor, but it was over within seconds and the wax effortlessly removed most of her hair on the first go. The strips are very sticky, so she reapplied it to the same area to ensure every last hair was yanked. She especially likes that the post-wax cloth feels very soothing on the skin, and that it helps remove any excess product and stickiness. Montemayor says her redness went away after about an hour, and she was hair-free for a good two weeks after that.

Hard wax kits tend to be messy when they’re applied or removed incorrectly. Remember to always apply a thin, even layer and pull the wax in the opposite direction of hair growth for a seamless waxing experience. However, the results are similar to those you would get at a waxing salon. This Sliick kit comes with a silicone cup and spatula, which makes the heating and application process a breeze. It takes a few rounds of heating and stirring the hard wax to get the right consistency. Once it starts looking like caramel, you’re ready to wax—and the waiting window is totally worth it because the hard wax is easy to maneuver and contains antioxidant-rich acai berry.

“Use a new stick each time you dip into the wax pot to avoid introducing bacteria, which could potentially cause infections,” says Gail Strong, an esthetician and CEO at Invigorate Spa in Indianapolis, Indiana.

The wax itself was easy to spread, but we found that it works best when laid in a thick layer, as thick as a banana peel. Montemayor likes that letting the wax cool completely before pulling the strip gives her a better result. The wax strip came up in one piece, lifting and removing all the hairs in its path. Unlike some of the hard wax kits we tried, this one didn’t leave any wax crumbs behind. Once you’re done waxing, all you have to do is let the wax in the cup and on the applicator dry, and it easily peels off. Montemayor found that after waxing her legs with this kit, it took about 10 days before she noticed the hair growing back.

Pro tip: Remember to dip a fresh stick into the wax pot to avoid introducing bacteria that can cause infections, says Strong.

Waxing tends to irritate the skin, but these strips from Billie were the most gentle of all the wax strips we tried. The sticky formula contains added castor oil, avocado oil, and aloe vera to soothe the skin, while the no-rub soft-gel wax attaches to every hair, whether it’s very fine or extra coarse.I used the Billie strips on my legs and underarms, and it was the least painful at-home waxing kit I tried. It’s a little tricky getting all of the hairs of my underarms, but the strips are very sticky, so I can go over the area two or three times and I’m left with smooth, hair-free pits. These strips didn’t leave behind wax on my skin, so cleanup is easy. I’ll just follow up with the included post-wax serum and my redness and minimal irritation are gone.The medium-sized wax strips are great for larger areas like the underarms and legs, but the small strips are too big to use on the upper lip or around the eyebrows. An easy hack is to trim them to fit your face—and with 32 wax strips in total, the $9 kit remains a great value.

Sometimes you just want a product that works for thousands of people. This all-inclusive kit earned a 4.4-star average from more than 38,350 Amazon reviews. More than 26,460 of them were perfect 5-star ratings. Casual.

So what makes it so impressive among Amazon shoppers? This kit includes quite literally everything you could need for a seamless at-home waxing experience. Waxing beads, an adjustable heat warmer, and 20 sticks for sanitary application? Of course. Skin prep spray and a soothing aftercare spray? Definitely. An instructional booklet with access to advice from a waxing expert via a smartphone app? Yup. It’s like the salon is truly in your bathroom.

Honestly, the biggest con about this device is that it requires some work. You’ve got to plug in the digital wax melt warmer and set the temperature; insert the wax bean bag into the removable waxing pot, and clean up the warmer and spatulas after. But TBH, based on the glowing Amazon reviews it’s a relatively small tradeoff worth the upkeep.

Women with sensitive skin or a low pain tolerance will love this sugaring wax because it’s gentle on the skin without compromising on hair removal. Its screw-on, roll-on applicator makes applying this wax a cinch, allowing you to reach tricky spots, like your chin or underarm, more precisely. You can easily wash the applicator after each use with soap and water. And to nourish the skin, the formula contains 100 percent organic virgin argan oil from Morocco.

Considering the above, it's no surprise that WH contributors love this buy, too. Its compact size is excellent for touch-ups on the go. And it’s a fantastic mess-free alternative that’s easy to apply and smells delicious, says Jackson. Plus, the wax works on shorter hairs as small as two millimeters, so it removes prickly stubble. While she fully recommends this at-home waxing kit, it’s worth noting that it’s not a hard wax, and it comes with cloth strips that may not cling to thicker hair types.

These Sally Hansen wax strips are infused with vitamin E and avocado oil for a more nourishing and less irritating waxing experience. The full-size strips are still large enough to cover a good amount of ground—like armpits and legs—and can leave you hair-free for up to eight weeks. You can also snip these strips to fit different areas of your face and body, including your underarms and bikini line.

Before Jackson switched over to laser hair removal, she always kept these strips on hand all the time. She used them for years and suggests putting a dish towel in the microwave for 20 seconds and placing the strip in the towel to warm it up before using it for better results. You can also follow up with a separate oil or serum, since it occasionally leaves a sticky residue on the skin that can be uncomfortable.

These waxing sticks are different from anything else we tried. Despite looking like something you would find in a kid's craft box, these don't play around when it comes to their ability to remove facial hair. The kit comes with two crayon-looking wax sticks, one small and one large. The small one is great for getting the errant hairs around your brows, while the larger stick is the perfect size for removing upper lip hair and peach fuzz on the rest of the face. Montemayor found that the stick made her feel like she had more control over where the wax went, which is especially important in sensitive areas like the face.To heat up the wax, all you need is a hair dryer. We recommend using the wax sticks in a bathroom because you’ll need to reheat the sticks often. The sticks are a little stringy, and the application can get messy because you’re trying to catch the wax and apply it before it continues dripping down the stick.

The hard wax has a pliable texture that snugly fits the curves of your face and can be applied in a nice, thick layer, which makes it easier to remove. We could do two to three swipes with the stick before we needed to blast it with the hair dryer again. The wax formula itself was very gentle and didn’t leave any sticky residue behind or tug at the top layer of skin. Overall, it was mostly painless because you’re working in such small sections. Once the stick dries, you can tuck it away for safekeeping and reuse it again the next time you need to remove your facial hair. We particularly like these sticks because they're travel-friendly, too. You can definitely throw them in a toiletry bag on your next weekend getaway.

With only three key factors to keep in mind, shopping for at-home waxing kits is refreshingly simple.

Before waxing, you should know there are two types of waxes: hard and soft.

If you want to use something stripless, go for hard wax. It adheres to the hair follicle (versus the skin), hardens, and can be removed on its own, eliminating the need for paper strips. For some, it may even feel less painful than soft wax, so it's great for sensitive skin, says dermatologist Nazanin Saedi, MD. The only caveat is that you may have to apply it several times in the same area to make sure all the hairs you target are removed.

Soft wax, on the other hand, is soft and applied in a thin layer. A paper strip is then used to adhere and remove the wax. Often, the top layer of skin is also removed, so it can be irritating for people with sensitive skin.

Ideally, beginners should look for kits that contain everything they need to get the job done—wax, strips, and finishing oil, at minimum. Novices may also appreciate waxing kits that come with pre-loaded strips, since they're less messy and require less precision. The tradeoff? You're limited to the size of the included strips, so look for kits with multiple sizes if you're targeting different areas of the body. Larger strips are fantastic for your legs, while small strips are practical for your face.

It's important to use the safest and gentlest wax kits available to avoid irritating, burning, and potentially scarring your skin. If you have sensitive skin, look for waxing kits that include skin-soothing ingredients, like castor and almond oils or aloe. And whatever you use, first test the wax in an area on your body that isn't too visible. This will allow you to see if it is gentle enough for your skin. If you experience a bad reaction, you'll know it's time to pivot to a different product.

For the past year, Women’s Health contributors and I, including Sabrina Talbert, Jasmine Gomez, Danielle Jackson, and Cristina Montemayor, tested the bestselling, most popular, and top-rated at-home waxing kits. Our team consulted dermatologists Blair Murphy-Rose, MD, Nazanin Saedi, MD, and Uchenna Okereke, MD, for pre-waxing advice and aftercare instructions to prevent irritation and promote healthy skin. Then, we got our hands on the kits and tested them in the comfort of our own homes, evaluating attributes like ease of use, comfort, results, and overall value. Of the 25 at-home waxing kits tested, the seven on this list delivered the best results in our in-depth evaluations.

At-home waxing removes body hair conveniently and cost-effectively, and the best kits do it quickly while minimizing pain and irritation. So, if you’re ready to ditch the razors, check out this list of the best waxing kits, tested by dermatologists and WH editors.

After waxing, you can prevent ingrown hairs from forming and minimize irritation immediately afterward by applying cool aloe to soothe skin, and sticking to loose clothes that won't create friction. "Aloe vera has anti-inflammatory properties that help soothe sunburned skin, while glycerin specifically can help to boost hydration levels to restore the skin's moisture barrier," dermatologist Divya Shokeen, MD, previously told WH in our guide to the best aloe vera gel. Some kits also come with nourishing oils and wipes to help minimize any post-wax irritation.

Before you head off to wax unwanted hair, these are a few other tips you should keep in mind.

Waxing removes hair by lifting it out at the root. With traditional waxing, hot wax is applied to skin and the hair is pulled off in the opposite direction of the way it's growing. The key word here and what can make at-home waxing dangerous is that it's hot.

“Hot wax can burn the skin—and it is a particularly dangerous type of burn because the hot product adheres to the skin,” says Dr. Murphy-Rose. Always make sure you're following the heating directions closely and that you hold your hand over the wax after it's been heated to gauge the temperature before applying it to your skin.

Then, first test the wax in an area on your body that isn't too visible. "That way you can check the temperature, but also see how your skin reacts," says Dr. Saedi. Testing a product will also allow you to see if it is gentle enough for your skin. “It's important to use the safest and gentlest wax kits available to avoid irritating, burning, and potentially scarring your skin," says Dr. Murphy-Rose. You should also avoid any ingredients you have a known allergy or sensitivity to. If you experience a bad reaction, you'll know it's time to pivot to a different product.

"Hot wax tends to adhere the strongest, so while it may remove hairs more efficiently, it can also stick to skin more and pull off those top layers of the skin as it's also pulling out your hair,” says Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Waxing exfoliates the top layer of skin and is more likely to cause hyperpigmentation a.k.a. dark spots, says Dr. Okereke. She says to think of the skin after waxing like a fresh, pink wound. "Ultraviolet rays are attracted to wounds, making the freshly waxed skin more susceptible to darkening as melanin (the dark pigment in skin) floods the area to try and protect it." Luckily, there is a simple fix: Wear broad-spectrum sunscreen! Better yet, keep that new skin out of the sun completely for at least a few days.

You'll also want to avoid any extra exfoliation, like retinol, chemical peels, and microdermabrasion, a few days prior and a few days following your at-home wax. A few other good things to know before getting started: Always wax on clean skin to avoid bacterial contamination in pores and make sure your hairs are long enough (at least 1/4 of an inch) to be grabbed by the wax.

The key to preventing ingrown hairs (an all too common downside of waxing for many) is to get the full hair follicle. The best way to do this is by keeping your skin taut and pulling the wax strip in the opposite direction of the way that your hair grows.

Sugaring, aka sugared wax or sugar gel, is generally safer because it’s applied to skin at room temperature (read: no risk of burning skin) and warms up with body heat. “Sugared ‘wax’ is not truly wax,” Dr. Murphy-Rose says. Rather, it’s a combination of sugar, lemon juice, and water. Some brands will infuse glycerin, fragrance, honey, or essential oils. Regardless of which brand you opt for, sugaring is water-soluble and easily rinses off the skin compared to hot wax, she says.

Sugaring and threading remove the hair follicle from the root but with less exfoliating, offering a gentler process, Dr. Okereke says. Though she warns that she's also had patients with coily-textured hair that still develop ingrown hairs and scarring from sugaring as well. The bottom line: "If you know you're prone to hyperpigmentation, ingrown hairs, or scarring, see a dermatologist to discuss the best hair removal practices for you," says Dr. Okereke.

#4686. There’s No Irony in The Armored League. Only Steel.

Welcome to NYC’s extremely violent, surprisingly wholesome new combat scene.

“THERE’S A LOT more work to do,” Damion DiGrazia muses, as 30 or so individuals spread themselves out across the gymnasium at the Manhattanville Community Center in Harlem. A pair of double doors swings lazily back and forth, marking a procession of students and the boxes they carry. DiGrazia leans against the wall, dressed in a red polo and khaki trousers, watching his small community unpack and ready itself for training.

The class does not have a format in the traditional sense. There is no lantern-jawed instructor with a whistle and a clipboard. No snap of uniforms in sync with the rhythm of a kata. There is not even, as far as I could tell, a formal warm-up. Instead, the room seems to have its own sense of internal order.

A group forms around the pieces of armor to begin the painstaking process of polishing and assessing each one for damage or repairs. Some—a breastplate, maybe a set of greaves—are singled out and ferried to a corner, where three individuals sit, cross-legged, and carefully hammer out the dents.

Ropes are thrown over the basketball hoops, and as soon as they land, students appear and begin practicing striking drills with blunted steel weapons. There are, admittedly, a lot of people with weapons. It’s a little surreal at first. When you encounter a fighter in full armor with a sword and buckler or a mace, there is a sense of visual cohesion. It is an entirely different matter to pass a fighter in cutoff denim and a T-shirt practicing elegant, sweeping strikes with an axe.

At the back of the room, the mats find their way into a rectangle, and small scrimmages begin with foam swords and shields. The training takes on its own rhythm; newer members train with foam swords and shields around the edges of the room, while the more seasoned fighters, now sporting what appear to be hockey helmets with face masks, begin grappling practice at its center. Everyone seems to know where they need to be and what they need to do.

It’s taken a long time to get here—years, actually, 13 of them, to be precise. After serving in the military, DiGrazia traces a path through Columbia University, then Harvard, before landing a job at Morgan Stanley. Finding the rhythm of corporate life increasingly dull, he sought relief through extreme sports. DiGrazia started with the classics: marathons, ultramarathons, scuba diving, skydiving, martial arts. But nothing really stuck; he was always chasing something else. That is, until a happy accident. DiGrazia tried what he thought was going to be “full-contact” LARPing (live-action role-playing), but found the experience less than fulfilling: “You couldn't punch people, couldn't grapple people, couldn't kick people, nothing,” DiGrazia says. The participants were wearing plastic armor, and a hit to the leg saw fighters taking a theatrical knee and swiping at their opponents. At the end of the practice, however, DiGrazia found himself sticking around, commiserating with another fighter, Zorikh, whom he credits as starting his journey along a path that would lead to him founding Gladiators NYC, and laying the groundwork for The Armored League.

Modern armored combat has a longer history in Europe, and DiGrazia found himself bouncing all over the continent, fighting in Poland or next to a castle in Spain. If you wanted to fight in armor, Eastern Europe was where you had to go. Stateside, the early days were decidedly underground and homebrew. Your options were more limited: small groups of fighters met in parking lots and cornfields. Orlando Mendez, one of the founding members of Gladiators NYC, remembers “a lot of horse arenas.” They were one of the few places you could throw someone into a wall without complaint. It was a sport that grew anywhere it could find space. Jason Puerta, owner of Golden Ring Combat, a West Coast armored combat group, recalls regularly fighting on the lawns of a corporate campus after securing the bemused blessing of the local security outfit. It wasn’t quite Fight Club—new members were always welcome (and still are), and people were encouraged to talk about it. Instead, the group could be said to be self-selective: “You either got the hang of it, or you just turned in your armor at the end of the day,” DiGrazia recalls. There were few rules, no weight divisions, and no weapon classes.

In these early years, the attrition rate was high. DiGrazia estimates about half of the participants quit within weeks. Even when he first secured the community center and started spreading the word about classes, he remembers sitting on a bench in the gym, staring at the doors, waiting for someone, anyone, to come to a class. Eventually, they did.

The free classes, access to equipment, loaner armor, and the open exhibition matches in New York’s Central Park—all of these, he believes, must remain core elements of the community and the sport. Gladiators NYC also has a nonprofit arm called “Santa’s Knights” where armored knights go door to door during the holidays and deliver presents to children. His commitment to this approach has not come without difficulties. DiGrazia once partnered with a martial arts school whose owner forbade him from sponsoring students who could not afford the $30 class fee. That school closed during COVID.

Technically, the sport can trace its roots back to the 14th century, when knights, foot soldiers, and men-at-arms would practice combat using dull steel weapons and a mixture of soft and plate armor. It was a way to hone their skills in times of peace. The fundamentals of the practice remain in a number of combat sports to this day, but one need only watch a bout of Olympic fencing (or “pointy tag” as Mendez described it) to realize the distance traveled. The Armored League, however, doesn’t seek a return to its medieval origins or even to the stringently historically accurate expressions, which tend to dominate in Europe. When pressed about this, DiGrazia gives an exasperated sigh: “I don't want some librarian walking around looking with a fucking magnifying glass on everybody's goddamn rivet. Leave us alone. Let's have a good time.” The aim is to bring the spectacle and joy to new audiences.

Even if, at first, you cannot follow the scoring, the fights are pure melodrama. Like any combat sport, the fighters’ stats are announced as they enter the ring—with one key distinction: their weight includes their suit of armor. Short of a quirk, it communicates the impact of the sport in a more visceral way: when a pair of combatants crash to the ground or bounce off the chain-link fencing, that’s close to 600 pounds of flesh and steel set in ballistic motion.

Bouts are divided into three to five one-minute rounds. Points are awarded based on strikes—where they land and how hard. Basic, clean strikes with weapons, shields, or fists get a base number of points. Meanwhile headshots, two-handed weapon strikes, and slugging a downed opponent get you even more. The bouts are judged by a panel set to one side of the ring, while a pair of counters runs frantically around the perimeter counting strikes.

There are comparatively few rules beyond some basic safety precautions: no stabbing or thrusting; no stomping; no strikes at the inner elbows, armpits, or the backs of knees; no slashing at the neck; and no submissions. Save for these, anything goes, and this adds to the thrill of the fights. Fighters are also not limited to their weapons, and in some cases, they will stand and trade blows like boxers. Though all of the serious fighters have broad and varied martial arts backgrounds—and training approaches—there's a roughly consistent path that leads to The Armored League. Snatches of Muay Thai knee strikes, judo sweeps, classical boxing, escrima, and BJJ are all visible in the blur of limbs, steel, and weapons. One can only imagine how the “librarians” would feel about that.

Strikes may come in flurries or great arcs, but most are hard enough to send sparks flying off the helmets. There is a marshal in the ring with the fighters, notably unarmored save for a yellow flag that’s mainly used to break the fighters up at the end of each round, which frequently ends in a tangle of armor and weapons on the floor of the ring.

There are two elements that, despite the passage of centuries, have not changed: cost and danger. Historians are divided on the exact conversion rate between 1400 and today, and most put it in terms of wages. They quote the cost of a full set of armor at somewhere between 12 and 18 months of pay. What’s universally agreed upon is that arms and armor were (and remain) anything but cheap. A full suit—then, as now—weighs anywhere from 60 to 80 pounds.

This century, prices start at around $5,000 and climb precipitously with customization. It can take anywhere from a few weeks to a year for delivery. Most participants build their suits over time as they are drawn deeper into the sport.

Building a full set is not easy. A cursory search online will lead you to a number of pages, which might appear to offer armor, but these sites are largely focused on cosplayers or LARPers. That armor will certainly hold together for a walk through Comic-Con, but it will do little to protect from a real blow. The handful of armorers still working today have long wait lists. Puerta notes that despite this, the communal nature of the sport means that much of the armor is passed down or traded between the combatants: as someone upgrades or hangs up their helmet, the armor finds its way into a new pair of hands or onto a new person’s shoulders. At Gladiators NYC, fighters who graduate from the classes, from “softs” (padded armor), and wish to try their hand at the real thing, can borrow pieces from Gladiators NYC’s own armory.

Amongst the current fighters who regularly participate in Armored League matches, almost all fight in custom armor. The suits must adhere to certain safety standards—thickness of steel, comprehensive eye protection, etc. But beyond that, there’s ample room for self-expression.

For example, Abeid “Mando” Mitchell fights in comparatively minimalist and lightweight armor and is readily recognizable by his distinctive helmet, which was made in the style of the Mandalorian from Star Wars. Luke “The Red Knight of Brooklyn” has assembled what he refers to as “a sporting replica” of 1480s armor in keeping with his own, more classical concerns.

Despite the care and attention each fighter devotes to their own armor, at all of the matches I attended, I saw weapons traded freely, shields swapped, even gauntlets lent. For as much violence as there is inside of a 60-second round, there is an equal, if not greater, level of care at the bell. The armor is not just for show; it’s for safety. Combatants want to win as much as they want to ensure their opponent walks off the field under their own power. It’s a fine balance, and as Mendez put it, “once you put on the armor and you get your ass beat a couple of times,” everybody is basically friends.

Nevertheless, it takes a toll. Puerta told me a story of how he almost lost his left eye when the tip of a sword slipped through the bars of his helmet. Others relayed stories of being crushed in a melee and of “helmet terrors” where breathing heavily in the confines of a helmet causes a buildup of carbon dioxide and creates a sensation similar to drowning.

What does the future look like? In my time with the League and Gladiators NYC, I sensed I was watching a sport in its adolescence. It is a league and community that seems to blink in the stark light of its own success and rapidly growing audience. Social media has made it easier for these once disparate communities to connect; the cornfields and horse rinks have been parlayed into an Octagon at the Melrose Ballroom in Queens or a showcase at a theater in Times Square. The bleachers that once held a smattering of friends and family have shifted into crowds drawn from all walks of life—at the sold-out show in Queens, the lines stretched around the block and some people waited an hour just to get into the venue. The Central Park exhibition matches, which happen every second Saturday of the month, have begun to draw crowds that can number over a thousand.

DiGrazia and his merry band have come a long way from the leaner years, when they struggled to find space to practice, the years when they fought in the parking lots of regional hotels in the Midwest or in the summer heat on the boardwalk in Coney Island.

Still, there is, for now, little to no money in this sport. The community, and the fighters too, all have day jobs. They are PhD students, fitness instructors, photographers, and graphic designers. One manages a magic and costume shop. Again, Fight Club springs to mind, as each goes about their day job, bearing the marks of a Thursday brawl or a weekend match, one can only wonder if anyone sees a bruise sticking out of a shirt sleeve and stops to ask just where it came from.

#4684. 16 Best Coffee Tables for Every Style and Budget (2026)

With their placement at the center of the living room, the best coffee tables can really unify the space—coming in every shape, size, and material you can think of. The hard part is browsing through pages and pages of options online to find the one that fits the vibe and style of your space—from smaller end table designs and nesting coffee tables to options made of reclaimed wood.

“While the most attractive furniture pieces aren’t always the most practical, Castlery’s Harper lift-top coffee table looks elevated and offers ample storage. One thing I’ll note is the piece is relatively heavy (about 125 pounds) and has no legs, so it might not be the easiest piece to move by yourself.” —Audrey Lee, shopping editor

“We first purchased this table in 2022 and own both the 38- and 28-inch versions. This met all those criteria and then some. Our son climbed on it, colored on it, and ran his cars and trucks over it daily, and it still looks great. Earlier this year, we purchased the second table for a different space. When it arrived, it was a bit high for our couch, so we had our building’s brilliant superintendent help us take a couple of inches off the legs. I don’t think a modification like that could successfully be done with a table of poor quality—this one survived the process beautifully and no one would ever be able to tell the difference.” —Shoko Wanger, AD contributor

No specific instructions, though it is treated with a waterborne lacquer surface treatment

Having experienced a quick tilt or two in my child-free household, I think my friend’s instincts were spot on. Here you’ll find even more coffee tables to maximize your space—some with glass top designs, travertine and marble beauties, plus choices for every design aesthetic imaginable. Think: High-quality, well-reviewed, aesthetically pleasing picks in a variety of styles, materials, and price ranges.

Visible knots in the exposed wood grain and subtle groves from the dovetail joinery are the only noticeable design details in Quince’s minimal table. Made of reclaimed oak, four available wood tones, including washed cream and deep black, are available to suit your living room’s existing palette. Well suited for a rustic aesthetic, the waterfall design accentuates the salvaged wood’s imperfections. From Lulu and Georgia’s collaboration with tastemaker Aimee Song, ripple effect legs bring a sculptural element to this low-profile table. It can perfectly accentuate your favorite area rug, or the media console you picked up from the brand to twin with Mandy Moore.

Use Arhaus’ puzzle-like Nolito table to bring warmth to your living room. There are two wood tones—a honey-hued light and mid-tone oak—that bring dimension to the overall look (think of it like mixing metals). Rounded joinery and gently beveled edges create smooth, uninterrupted lines throughout, with the two flat top tiers connected by artfully angled wood pieces. Providing lots of open storage, the bottom tier has ample space to house your coffee table books or keep your candle inventory out of plain sight.

While we lauded the rise of printed sofas earlier this year, this maximalist coffee table is an equally charming way to incorporate pattern play into your living room. The plinth-style table has serious main character energy, with a low-profile block design that isn’t afraid to command space. We recommend pairing the table with even more stripes (maybe writer Julia Harrison’s Schoolhouse sofa?) or different patterns to create a richly layered space.

This mid-century inspired style stands out for its reverse-tapered legs. Made from kiln-dried solid wood, this is a sturdy, easily-assembled piece that keeps your coffee table stylish. Some big art books and a sculptural detail, and you've got a fully realized design moment on your hands.

This Ikea table is a true budget-friendly option that has almost 300 five-star reviews to its credit. It has a rust-resistant galvanized steel body, with a streamlined mesh top that works even outdoors since water passes through it like a sieve. Reviewers liked that the piece was easy to assemble (like most of the brand’s furniture, in our experience), and that the size makes it suitable for smaller yards and patio decks. Some also noted that inventory tends to go in and out of stock (especially in the summer months), so we’d recommend ordering now while it’s ready to ship. warranty, too.

The Shou Sugi Ban coffee table from House of Leon is our pick if you’re aiming for an austere, wabi-sabi aesthetic. Unlike other mass-produced styles, the beauty of this piece lies in the ancient Japanese technique of charring wood, a process which reveals a refined, hardened finish to the grain after successive rounds of burning. Each piece possesses a distinct finish and asymmetry, so no two are exactly alike.

In the category of discreet storage, Article’s Karl table brings its A game. The lift-top mechanism brings versatility and hidden storage (just think of all the scented candles that will finally have a place to call home), while the streamlined design is easy to incorporate into any space, whether you’re looking to accentuate a coastal theme or collecting more Japandi-leaning decor this year. A versatile range of finishes—white oak, medium smoked oak, and a deep walnut hue—also ensures your pick aligns with your wood preferences.

For the burl-skeptics, this round top-pick from AD100 honoree firm Pierce & Ward feels like a conscious toe-dip rather than a radicalized nose dive. The inlay detail offers just a hint of texture, while the surrounding oak veneer and modern, rounded legs distinctly appeal to the more minimally-minded design connoisseurs among us.

Anointing your living room with a Noguchi coffee table won’t go unnoticed by serious designheads: It’s a piece that underscores any collector’s proclivity for modern design. The sculptural legs are the star of the show, but don’t underestimate the power of a good area rug—a glass coffee table serves as a nice visual anchor to a graphic design underfoot.

The softened edges of this bronzed table create a silhouette we’d describe as delicately industrial. A handsome leather sofa might help play up the textural elements of the distressed finish, or you could lean into contrasts with a clean-looking beige or tasteful performance linen.

Following the rule of thumb for all furniture, you’ll want at least a foot of breathing room around your coffee table to keep a comfortable walkway. Most retailers, like Castelry, recommend a two-thirds approach to measuring—meaning that your coffee table should be no longer than two-thirds the length of your sofa. While the standard height for coffee tables is between 16 and 18 inches, if your sofa is lower (like a classic Togo) or taller, you may want to adjust for a more comfortable foot rest and arm reach.

From wood and metal to stone and acrylic, there are plenty of material options for you to navigate on your buying journey. Stone coffee tables are ideal for those looking to make a design statement. Just consider the drama that an intricately veined marble surface can add to a moody and modern living room, like in Harris Reed’s London home. A wood coffee table is the most design agnostic: Choose a rich wood tone to lean more mid-century or a natural oak for a minimalist, Scandi feel. Wood coffee tables are known to show water stains and scuffs more than glass or stone, so ensuring you have the right cleaners is key to longevity. In small spaces, a glass or acrylic coffee table can provide an optical illusion, taking up minimal visual real estate while still giving you a surface to set down a drink or burn your favorite candle.

#4682. Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.

But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.

Nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.

Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:

Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.

That’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.

But it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:

October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.

China’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.

Tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.

Meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.

Through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:

The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.

Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.

So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.

As we reported last month, Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We said to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.

We’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers. Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.

We don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

I've been saying this for the last two years. Tesla's problem isn't that Elon temporarily alienated customers in Europe or other countries. Yes that killed sales for a bit, but in the end people are practical and will buy the best car for the money. And we saw that is exactly what happened with European Tesla sales coming back when gas prices rose and Tesla as a package (quality + price) was still very competitive.

The real problem that Tesla has is that they're falling behind in China not because anyone cares about Elon's politics, but because the cars are just less and less competitive. And while the Chinese competition doubles down on vehicle development and rolls out a new car every week, Tesla has lost all interest in it. There is absolutely nothing on the horizon for them in terms of new vehicles that consumers can buy. Looks like the 3 and Y are all they will have and no updates are coming.

I know, FSD or bust, but that's also assuming Chinese brands don't crack that nut at the same time.

Two things can be true at once. The export numbers show Tesla front-loading shipments ahead of the rebate cut. And Chinese demand for a Model 3 and Model Y lineup that hasn’t fundamentally changed in years keeps fading while Xiaomi, Leapmotor and BYD launch new models every few months.

And if Tesla is choosing to send cars abroad instead of selling them in China, that’s not exactly a vote of confidence in its Chinese business either.

The real test is November and December. Last year, Tesla bounced back to 73,000 and 94,000 domestic sales. If it gets close to that again, October was mostly timing. If it doesn’t, Tesla has a serious problem in the world’s largest EV market, and the export valve that’s been hiding it gets more expensive in April.

If you’re buying an EV, Chinese-built or not, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4681. 11 Best Dining Tables to Elevate Take-Out Nights (2026)

Even if you order takeout (almost) every evening, the best dining tables can make all of the difference for elevating your dishes, down to the cold leftovers you’ve reheated for dinner. You don’t have to be a regular hostess to know that these furniture pieces are more than a place to eat; they double as a surface to display your latest tableware finds, function as a desk, and even help facilitate conversation. Whether you’re looking to outfit a quaint breakfast nook or source something with panache for a formal dining area, the best dining tables bring in just the right amount of personality without distracting from what’s actually important—the people you’re eating with.

Ahead, we’re highlighting our 11 favorites, from a perfectly mod pedestal to an extendable farmhouse beauty. Looking for a dining table that was made for small spaces? We have options for you too.

Paired with the Meja dining chairs, Article’s Plumas table helped senior shopping editor Nashia Baker convert an empty living room nook into a dining setup. With slightly angular legs and rounded corners, the table evokes a classic, midcentury silhouette (fitting perfectly with the rest of Baker’s apartment aesthetic). The extendable feature is accessible simply by pulling a latch underneath the table and sliding either end apart. With the table pushed against the wall, she says her “current setup works just fine to comfortably seat three people.” Baker does plan on using the extendable design during larger holiday parties “so there’s plenty of space for a potluck-style tablescape.”

West Elm’s Miles dining table was the investment shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher needed to fully maximize guest seating in her Brooklyn apartment. “I love playing host—poker nights, RuPaul’s Drag Race watch parties, you name it. An extendable table was an ideal solution to seat extra guests for a dinner party while not eating up extra square footage on a regular day,” she says. In the 60 to 80” size, Arzbaecher can sit up to 10 guests around the table (though it requires some squishing onto the matching bench). With a modern, rounded silhouette, the double-edge detailing along the sides of the tabletop perfectly complements the equally curvy dining chairs the producer already owned. And despite its substantial appearance, the table is surprisingly agile. “Don’t let the chunky look deceive you,” she says. “This table isn’t heavy, and I’ve been able to move the leaf in and out on my own with ease.”

With a vibe that falls somewhere along the spectrum of an upstate farmhouse and Spanish revival, this rectangular dining table from Green Row charmed commerce writer Julia Harrison with its extendable surface and rich wood stain. “This table does the work of modern design at its best: It looks completely authentic—like it was lifted from a small rural French farm, dusted off, and dropped in my dining room in Brooklyn,” she says. Extended, she notes that it comfortably fits eight people, and has paired it with some dark wood Windsor chairs to create an overall farmhouse-esque effect. “It's the sort of table that makes you want to host things, the way good writing can inspire you to write,” she adds.

Strikingly modern and architectural, the Aava dining table from Wayfair is the ideal budget pick for those still looking to make a major design impact. Pedestal tables boast timeless design appeal thanks to their streamlined build and versatile aesthetic (it’s part mod, part midcentury, part Scandi—this table fits anywhere). Whether it’s just you in your apartment or a Thanksgiving-level gathering, this oval dining table offers a number of sizes to accommodate your friends and family. The sturdy, oval pedestal base ensures no drinks are spilled as you maneuver in and out of your seat, while the thin tabletop leaves ample room for all chair heights and seat positions.

For small apartment dwellers or those looking to finally stop eating meals on the couch, a space-saving bistro table is the way to go. The high-gloss finish is a dramatic (and welcome) reprieve from the traditional wood surfaces that characterize the genre.

Great for small dining spaces and eat-in kitchens, a drop-leaf silhouette offers a kind of versatility not seen in traditional dining tables. This best-seller from Pottery Barn has a rectangular frame with two sections that lower to create a smaller square for everyday use. The leaves also include additional supports that can lock into place for added stability.

This one from West Elm can collapse both sides to sit flush with the wall and save valuable floor space in small apartments (even the legs fold in). Extend one side only if it’s just you, or sit four dining chairs comfortably with a 42-inch diameter at full size.

As seen in the Hollywood Hills home of TV writer and producer Cameron Johnson, this CB2 dining table has a streamlined, Brutalist feel with its offset legs. This solid wood dining table is available in both 63 inches (best for seating four to six) and 91 inches (best for six to eight seats).

#4679. The coolest ride in town is England’s first electric ice cream truck

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it says it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

It’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, says this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”

We’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?)

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison says it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.

#4677. A Fantastical Perch Above Toulon’s Old Port, Where Mermaids Meet Mediterranean Light

Though perhaps not well known outside France, Vincent Darré is one of Paris’s most familiar figures—always on the scene, day and night. The impish designer rarely just enters a room; he bounces in, impeccably dressed, with an infectious laugh and beautiful manners. At home in the worlds of fashion, society, art, and design, he is welcome at every table, always ready with a clever remark, a kind word, and no shortage of creative energy.

From his early days in fashion, which included stints at Moschino and Ungaro and a close, yearslong collaboration with none other than Karl Lagerfeld, Darré has followed a singular path, turning his creative energies to furniture and interiors with the opening of his own studio, Maison Darré, in 2008. A pair of recently completed Paris hotels—L’Aventure, at the foot of the Arc de Triomphe, and Hôtel Le Magnifique, in the heart of Montparnasse—are propelling him onto the design scene in a bigger way than ever. His work has long encompassed scenography and ephemeral installations, among them crowd-pleasing turns at AD Intérieurs, the erstwhile annual showcase hosted by AD France.

In the formal salon, a pair of carved wood armchairs with inlaid stone backs have seat cushions of a Dedar fabric. Darré-designed objects include his Calder table, Minos rug, and Lyre mirror. He also created the trompe-l’oeil pilasters topped with 18th-century gilded wooden capitals. Late-19th-century French lantern; 1940s Italian ceramic dolphin table.

In the guest bedroom, Darré sits on an 18th-century gilded wood bench upholstered in velvet by Métaphores. A Darré-painted mural frames the 18th century Italian headboard upholstered in Tony Duquette’s Xanadu fabric for Jim Thompson. The bedcover and cushions are from Darré’s collection for Monoprix.

Darré was born in Paris, in the 14th, and went to school there as a boy. When his parents separated in the 1970s, his father—a sociologist—moved to the Luberon, and Vincent went with him; not long after, his mother, unwilling to live far from her son, also moved south, to Montpellier. “This allowed me to be Parisian, but also one who knew other places,” he says. It’s a telling detail: the South of France has informed his eye ever since, with its particular sense of light, water, and ease. Though he first went to school for fashion, his real love was drawing, as it had been since childhood. “Sometimes people are surprised,” he notes, “that a finished work of mine is almost always exactly like I had drawn it.”

After a series of Paris apartments over the years, Darré has recently acquired a getaway in Toulon, the Mediterranean port city. The attraction was immediate. He had been invited to preside over the jury of Design Parade, the summer design festival held in Toulon and Hyères, and the city seized him the moment he arrived. “Once I got to the airport, in 2017, I immediately felt I was home. Chez moi! I had never experienced that feeling before.” He kept an eye on the listings and, after a few false starts, found exactly what he wanted.

In the entrance, Darré’s Vase Soleil stands atop a 1940s Venetian console table against a wall decorated with trompe l’oeil caryatids.

A 19th-century rattan sofa upholstered in Jean Lurçat’s Sirenes fabric by Pierre Frey.

Overlooking the Toulon harbor, the primary bedroom’s office area features several Darré designs including his Orphée sconce, Singez-moi table lamp, the carved and lacquered wood desk, a Vertebré chair cushioned in a fabric by Pierre Le-Tan, and a Column stool.

Lion head mascarons flank the doorway into the primary bedroom. 1970s plaster Buddha lamps with Darré-painted shades stand atop 17th-century French consoles. A 1960s plaster seahorse is displayed in the fireplace.

The apartment occupies the top floor of a little three-story house overlooking the fishing port—a compact 860 square feet with stunning views of the sea. It was already lovely when he moved in, all white, with nothing architectural to be done: the perfect backdrop for Darré and his pencils and paints. He brought many of his favorite things—collections, objects, and furniture gathered over the years, added to since at the Drouot auction house and the little brocantes he loves to haunt. Furnishing was, he says, a gradual process, bringing in pieces little by little and slowly making the space his own over time.

Darré’s Crocodile bench stands in the primary bedroom. Two-Faced lamps with hand-painted shades atop Pas Gigogne tables flank the bed, and his Poisson bookcase is at left. The plaster chandelier is by Mathieu Challières, and the plaster unicorns are from a set designed by Jean Cocteau.

A metal figure given to Darré by Ines de la Fressange stands next to his Singez-moi lamp on the office area desk.

Darré’s Tabou shelf in the primary bedroom

Darré on his Column stool with a 19th-century gilt-wood mirror from a Paris flea market

Darré speaks often of his love for Toulon, and of Jean Cocteau, who adored this coast and painted frescoes nearby. “I like the sweetness of life here,” he says. “Nothing has really changed since the 1950s. It’s the Provence of another era.” Every little square has its fountain; everyone is kind. It’s a military port, but its douceur de vie is what holds him.

The apartment represents Vincent Darré to a T: not an unadorned surface in sight, a home full of memories, tributes, and joy. “This has been one of my dreams, to have a house on the water,” he says. “My place in Paris is exactly the same, though not on the water. But both are little suspended palaces. I create my own follies.” From the painted columns flanking the windows—among his very first purchases, which have followed him from home to home—to the mermaids and sea creatures and the tented bed, everything belongs to the fantastical world of Darré. As one of his teachers observed early on, you could recognize his hand from the very start.

A close-up of Darré’s ceramic Two-Faced lamp

The dining area features a red lacquer table and chairs with Darré’s Dolphin lamp in the corner.

That world is entirely his own. He draws on a lineage of great fantasists—Charles de Beistegui, Henri Samuel, Jean Cocteau, Christian Bérard, Tony Duquette—yet the result, for all its jumble, is rigorously coherent. His flourish is always present. As the actress Isabelle Adjani once told him, to enter one of his interiors is to step into one of his drawings. Which is exactly what he wants.

For all the bounce in his step, Darré is no one’s fool. He knows we live in difficult times, and likes the idea of adding a flourish of fantasy to reality. “I have my little world—a dream universe, but one you can live in.” He loves to dance, and even took tap-dancing lessons as a teenager, all the better to channel Fred Astaire or Gene Kelly. “Life is a film, and we are the actors,” he says. “That’s why I always dress the way I do.” Lights, camera, action—Darré is always ready.

#4675. Hästens 2000T Mattress, Tested and Reviewed (2026)

From the moment I touched down in Sweden, the focus was on sleep. Coming off a red-eye flight from New York with only two hours of rest (three if we’re being generous), there was nothing more I wanted to do than lie down. Luckily, a Hästens mattress—the reason for my trip—awaited me at the hotel and soon provided what was perhaps the most luxurious nap I’d ever experienced.

The Swedish manufacturer, which has been making beds since 1852, sits atop the luxury market for mattresses. The brand—whose name is Swedish for “the horse’s”—has a consuming commitment to craftsmanship, and its horsehair-filled beds are handmade. That level of focus also comes with a hefty price tag, which is why the brand is perhaps best known by the general public for its presence in celebrity homes (or possibly its cameo in an Emily in Paris episode as the subject of the titular character’s latest marketing campaign). But reputation aside, Hästens knows how to make a damn good bed.

But what earns a mattress luxury status? And what is it actually like to sleep on one from Hästens? After touring the brand’s main factory in Köping, Sweden, I’ve laid my head on one of its most popular mattresses, the 2000T, for the last few months, all in the name of trying to understand how much money a good night’s sleep is worth.

To the average person, horsehair is likely not the first mattress fill material that comes to mind—if it comes to mind at all. Gel, innerspring, memory foam, cotton, or some combination of those are way more common. But horsehair has a historic precedent, having been used in beds for many periods of human history, particularly when horses were the primary mode of transportation.

Much of the present-day reason for using the material comes from a scientific point of view: Horsehair strands are naturally hollow, which Hästens claims “transports any excess heat and moisture from your body during deep sleep.” Additionally, when cut and treated, the strands form a helix shape, which works in conjunction with the metal springs in a bed for a strong base of support.

Exterior of the Hastens factory in Köping, Sweden, designed by British architect Ralph Erskine.

An hour and a half train ride northwest from Stockholm, the small town of Köping is so quiet, you might expect to see a horse roaming the streets—maybe having recently received a haircut to donate to the mattress cause. When thinking of the word factory, one may expect a loud, gigantic warehouse filled with whirring machines and assembly lines moving so quickly you can hardly see the product before it whizzes past. But the Hästens factory possessed a quite different vibe. Sure, there is still machinery and expansive production areas, but it was fairly quiet, and I felt that the energy was more akin to a pottery studio than an industrial plant: craft-forward, methodical, and with a focus on handmade artistry. In fact, my host told me that only around 100 people work in the main factory, most of whom are from the area, highlighting the company as a point of pride for the local community.

Walking into the processing room of the factory, I was greeted by a small mountain of horsehair on the floor. It looked much more like a soft version of steel wool than the shiny mane and tail I was envisioning. That’s because the hair is cut down to small strands prior to being integrated into the mattresses. The hair also goes through several disinfecting and processing treatments before it even arrives at the factory. Taking a clump between my hands, I was surprised by its springiness. (And horse girls need not fear about animal welfare: My host for the trip confirmed that their suppliers from farms around the world aren’t killing horses for their hair, the mane and tail cuttings they receive are ethically sourced.)

The blue check pattern, developed by fourth-generation company leader Jack Ryde in 1978, is synonymous with the brand. So much so that a check-laden Mercedes was waiting to drive us from the train station to the factory.

Each layer of horsehair in the mattress is fluffed by hand and placed between sheets of cotton and wool.

Every aspect of the bed creation process happens by hand: prepping the layers of wool and horsehair for the filling, arranging and securing steel springs, framing the Swedish pine base. I watched workers build each part of the bed with a devoted level of care. The only fully automated aspect of the bed manufacturing that I witnessed on my tour was stitching a pattern onto the top mattress to give it a signature tufted texture. But even that is hand-sewn on certain bed models.

Quality is tested at every step, and if something isn’t up to par, production restarts. For some models, including the Grand Vividus (at the top of Hästens range), there are only a select few craftspeople who are trained in the production process. Much of the brand’s higher price tag comes down to that heightened level of labor and care. If someone on the team is sick or is simply just working slower on a given day, the production timeline increases to accommodate the quality level that Hästens demands: perfection.

My loaned mattress also included a full set of Hästens bedding.

The 2000T is one of the brand’s best sellers, falling around the middle of their price range.

When it comes to my sleep setup, my mattress was the element that I’d been putting off upgrading for years. I only leveled up my years-old box spring with a mattress topper a few years ago. I tend to prioritize bedding when buying new duds for the bedroom, and because I’m consistently testing various sets of sheets for AD, my focus tends to be on how linens can visually transform a space rather than shift my physical experience. All to say, upgrading to a Hästens was like going from a hand-me-down sedan to a Lamborghini.

Before receiving the loaned mattress for testing, I tried out different models in person at the Manhattan flagship store in NoMad, an experience Hästens coins the Sleep Spa. As a staff member talked me through proper spinal alignment and important pressure points, I lay on various models in a Goldilocks-esque journey to see which mattress was the right fit. True to Hästens’ superlative level of service, even this part of the process felt curated. Ambient music played, lights dimmed, and I was given two pillows and a duvet for snuggling. The meditative process made me focus on how my body responded to each mattress. As a combination stomach-and-side sleeper—and someone who likes to sit on her bed—I selected the 2000T (in firm) after around an hour of sampling.

Despite being a firmer model, the 2000T still contours to my body in a way that I can only describe as cushy. The horsehair filling provides a unique springiness that the compression of memory foam or cotton can’t quite replicate. It sinks in just enough to give my shoulders enough space when I sleep on my side, but is supportive enough to keep my hips from dropping out of alignment for the nights I’m on my stomach.

As I mentioned, I often lounge on bed to read, play video games, or what have you. While facilitating sleep is the primary function of a mattress, I was keen to see how its edge control and support would stand up to this alternative usage. I was surprised by how little back pain I sustained after reading sessions that extended beyond two hours. Because of its reinforced springs at the corners and edges, I could also sit right on the edge of the mattress without feeling like I was going to roll off.

The aspect of the horsehair fill I was most intrigued to test was its claim of moisture and heat-wicking properties. I like to be fully swaddled underneath my duvet, top sheet, and sometimes even another blanket when I sleep, which can be a recipe for waking up sweaty. That hasn’t happened once with the 2000T. The foam topper on my prior bed often trapped heat, and I’d wake up in the middle of the night to rip off some of the layers of bedding in order to cool down. With the Hästens, though, I can be as greedy with my bedding as I want to be without overheating.

The ‘massage’ portion lasted about 10 minutes.

As part of their high bar of customer service, the company offers a free recalibration program from select stores to help maintain the longevity of the mattress and mitigate any compression issues. The product care program involves Hästens staffers visiting your home (typically once a year) to flip and massage the mattress—the latter consisting of a person marching back and forth across the mattress to redistribute the fill materials. I can safely say having a grown man in booties walk in circles on top of my bed for 10 minutes was one of the oddest moments of my life, but sleeping on the bed that night, I could feel the difference. While there weren’t any severe lumps formed in my two-month testing period, the process smoothed out any compression in the areas I most often lay.

Although I’ve only slept on the 2000T for around two months, I can see a noticeable change in how my body feels after a night’s rest. I struggle with hypermobility and have a family history of arthritis, so I’m on high alert about how my joints feel upon waking up in the morning. On my old bed, I typically awoke with some pain in my hips and a stiff lower back. While sleeping on the Hästens hasn’t fully eliminated any achiness, I essentially ceased needing to do the typical stretching routine I used to perform in the morning in order to get my body ready for the day.

Down pillows were provided by the brand for my loaner bed.

The structure of Hästens beds includes a top mattress and middle mattress, the former mimicking a thick topper.

As someone who has notoriously bad nighttime habits (like plentiful screen time), I had accepted I’d only be able to expect a low level of restfulness from my sleep. I was content with a solid six hours and low-level of back achiness in the morning, thinking I couldn’t consistently adjust my routine to improve my experience. Sleeping on the Hästens 2000T has changed that mindset drastically. It’s without a doubt the best mattress I’ve ever slept on.

However, it’s easy for me to say this bed is worth it because I didn’t have to pay the steep price tag of $74,780 to try it out in my home. Yes, Hästens exceeded my expectations when it came to sleep, but after the testing period ends, I don’t anticipate a sudden change in my finances that would allow me to invest in my own 2000T. Although the brand’s beds are built to last a lifetime, and we spend a third of our lives asleep, the question of how much a good night’s sleep is really worth is highly individualized.

This experience more broadly made me consider where we are most willing to invest in when it comes to our home spaces. Sure, a covetable mattress like one from Hästens may not be as flashy as other big-ticket purchases, like a giant flat screen, but I’d posit a splurge has few better use cases than on something you return to each night.

#4673. Juiced unveils another lower-cost moto-styled electric bike: Scrambler Core

Juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a new, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core. The new bike keeps much of the moto-inspired styling and performance of the existing Scrambler Hardtail, but trims back several components to knock several hundred dollars off the price.

The new Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.

Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.

Teens are a major part of the moto-style e-bike market, and Juiced has designed its Scrambler e-bikes as a safer option for those younger riders. In addition to ensuring street-legal performance for most major markets, Juiced rolled out a feature known as Speed Lock, which is essentially a parental control option that lets a parent or guardian set a lower speed limit using a PIN code that prevents their teen from later modifying the speed limit.

The launch comes as part of the rebirth of Juiced Bikes following the brand’s acquisition last year. The company was founded in 2009 and was acquired in 2025 by the co-founders of Lectric Ebikes, who have since brought the brand back with a new generation of its popular Scrambler platform.

The biggest changes appear to be in the powertrain, battery, brakes, and suspension.

The standard Scrambler Hardtail launched earlier this year set the standard for the flagship models by using a 750W nominal motor with 90 Nm of torque and reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). Its 52V 19.2Ah battery provides nearly 1 kWh of capacity and a claimed range of up to 60 miles (96 km).

The Scrambler Core steps down to a 500W nominal rear hub motor rated for 1,176W peak and 80 Nm of torque. Top speed is also reduced slightly to 25 mph (40 km/h), while the throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h). Importantly, though, Juiced has retained its 52V architecture, meaning this is still a fairly punchy setup rather than a dramatically detuned budget bike.

Battery capacity takes a hit as well. The standard Core gets a 52V 10Ah battery with 520 Wh of capacity, rated for up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Spending another $200 gets the Core Long-Range with a 52V 15Ah, 780Wh battery and a claimed 60-mile (96 km) maximum range. As with nearly all e-bikes, expect real-world range to fall short of the idealized advertised numbers, which are generally only achievable under the lowest power pedal assist.

Juiced also traded the Talon P4 four-piston hydraulic brakes found on the more expensive Scrambler for Talon P2 two-piston brakes. The KKE inverted fork with 140mm of travel is gone too, replaced by a more conventional aluminum triple-crown fork with 100mm of travel.

Those are meaningful downgrades, but they’re also largely the kinds of changes I’d expect to see when trying to shave $300 off an already competitively priced moto-style e-bike. It’s a strategy we’ve seen play out before in the industry, helping lower costs for riders who want a flagship bike but don’t necessarily want to pay flagship prices.

Even so, important features remain to help maintain the look and feel of the Juiced Scrambler line. The Core still gets 20 x 4-inch fat tires, hydraulic disc brakes, a frame-integrated TFT display, four pedal-assist levels, a headlight, taillight, brake light, and turn signals. It’s a single-speed setup and weighs 73 lb (33 kg), while being rated for a 300 lb (136 kg) payload.

Perhaps the more interesting addition is the Scrambler Core Midsize.

While the regular Core is recommended for riders 5’2” and taller, the Midsize drops that figure to just 4’10”. Pricing remains the same: $1,399 with the 520Wh battery or $1,599 with the 780Wh long-range pack.

And with an eye towards safety, the Core and Core Mini retain Juiced’s PIN-protected parental speed lock. Parents can set the motor-assisted top speed anywhere from 1-25 mph and lock the setting behind a four-digit PIN. That makes even more sense on the Midsize version, which seems tailor-made for younger riders who want the moto-style look but may not yet comfortably fit the larger Scrambler.

The Core is launching in several decidedly Juiced color names, including Black Nectar, Fruit Punch, Sour Grape, White Grape, Berry Freeze, and Blood Orange, though availability varies between frame sizes and battery configurations. Juiced says preorders are expected to begin shipping around the end of the month.

At $1,399, the Scrambler Core feels like a logical extension of Juiced’s rebooted lineup. You lose some battery, motor power, braking hardware, suspension travel, and a few mph compared to the Hardtail, but the underlying recipe is largely intact. For riders who mostly want the Scrambler look and feel – or parents shopping for a smaller rider – saving $300 may be a pretty compelling trade. Especially when you consider that the original Juiced Scrambler already led the industry in value for moto-style e-bikes from reputable brands.

Toss in the strong backing from Lectric and the 3-year warranty, and it’s hard to consider much else among the competition.
