#4625. In medieval Italy, a spider bite could send you into a dancing frenzy

Published Nov 10, 2026 9:01 AM EST

There’s a chance that if you visited southern Italy during the Middle Ages, you might happen upon a port town where people were dancing uncontrollably in the streets. You’d find them frantically spinning, jumping…even crawling on the ground. But unlike the broader “dancing mania” that was taking place across Europe at the same time, this dance, dubbed the “tarantella,” was more than a sickness. It was also a cure.

“Some people say that the bite of a spider caused people to tremor and shake,” Anna Harsh, a professional dancer and founder of the Allegro Dance Company, which specializes in Italian folk dances, tells Popular Science. They’d then continue moving to sweat out the poison.

Tarantism, a historical psychological and social phenomenon that led to anxiety, melancholia, and uncontrollable movement, ran rapidly throughout southern Italy from the 11th to the 17th century.

The epicenter of tarantism was Taranto, a coastal city in southern Italy’s Puglia region, which occupies the “heel” of the country’s boot shape. Each summer harvest season, local residents would spend long days working in the fields where large, hairy wolf spiders burrowed.

Most people believed that these wolf spiders carried a toxic venom. If they bit you, tarantism would quickly set in. The only cure would be to sweat out the venom through continuous, fast-paced dancing. We’re talking uncontrollable, flailing movements that would eventually exhaust both the dancer and the illness.

Although southern Italy was the epicenter of tarantism, similar outbreaks of involuntary, convulsive dancing occurred throughout the Middle Ages. The first major recorded frenzy began on June 24, 1374 in Aachen, Germany. Soon after, others followed in countries like Switzerland and modern-day France. In many of these cases, those afflicted danced uncontrollably for days or weeks. Some even died dancing. Since these events happened centuries ago, no one really knows what caused them. But the tarantism of southern Italy and its ensuing tarantella dance both seem unique.

The name “tarantula” may have originated with the wolf spiders (Lycosa tarantula) of Taranto, but wolf spiders and tarantulas belong to two entirely different spider families. Still, with a leg span that can reach up to three to four inches across, multiple sets of eyes, and a series of odd, jerky movements when they walk, wolf spiders make easy targets for conspiracy theories and urban legends.

While they can look frightening, science has determined over the years that a wolf spider’s bite is generally harmless to humans. Symptoms appear more like a mild bee sting, with a bit of localized pain and swelling, then a full-blown disco dance party. In fact, among the world’s 38,000 known spider species, only about 100 species have venom that is detrimental to humans.

In 1976, a college paper blamed the Salem witch trials on moldy bread. It wasn’t true.

Ancient Romans thought drinking gladiator blood could cure epilepsy

In medieval France, murderous pigs faced trial and execution

4 times drinking coffee was illegal—or even punishable by death

The mysterious dancing plague that killed people in 1518

The radioactive ‘miracle water’ that killed its believers

In August 1693, an anonymous Neapolitan doctor even tested the connection between the bite of a wolf spider and tarantism. He let two wolf spiders bite him in a public experiment, but the doctor never broke out into fancy footwork.

Instead, modern science shows that the extreme summer heat, physical stress, dehydration, and even ample wine drinking could have easily caused the symptoms of tarantism. Still, the wolf spider and tarantism remain undisputedly linked.

Sometimes called the “Dance of the Spider,” the tarantella began as a ritual healing dance that aimed to sweat out any venom associated with tarantism. Many versions of the tarantella exist today, though they’re more traditional folk dances than medical treatments. Instead, the  ‘tarantella as cure’ dance is more formally known as the pizzica. The word pizzica comes from the Italian verb pizzicare, which means “to pinch” or “to bite.”

“Today we might think of that ‘bite’ as something internal, like stress or anxiety,” says Harsh. Picture when someone you know suddenly loses a loved one and they’re shaking uncontrollably. “That person will dance or move and do whatever they can to help them get through that situation.”

Pizzica tarantata is performed almost like an exorcism, the spiritual practice of evicting demons or malevolent entities (such as supposed spider’s venom) through a sort of ritual—in this case, ecstatic, free-form dance.

Musicians gathered around the inflicted victim, playing incessant, fast-paced 6/8-tempo rhythms driven by a tambourine, violins, and guitars. The person suffering from tarantism would then “go into a trance,” says Harsh. “There was shaking, hopping, swirling, and turning. Some people would roll on the ground and come back up. The pizzica has movements, but you can put them in any order. It’s however the spirit moves you.”

These days, most historians and scientists agree that wolf spiders didn’t cause tarantism. Rather, tarantism was a form of mass hysteria, a situation where a group of people share the same intense fear, anxiety, or physical sickness—like dizziness, shaking, or stomach aches—even though there is no real physical or medical grounds for it.

Tarantism mostly afflicted impoverished individuals, particularly women (tarantatas). One possible reason: “Women were oppressed and faced plenty of inequality,” says Harsh. “Dance is a way that they could express themselves, even scream, through movement. That they could be the center of attention for just a minute and be seen.”

Over the centuries, the tarantella has become a celebration of life and joy rather than a frantic ritual. Italians often perform this now-beloved folk dance at weddings and festivals.

Every August, La Notte della Taranta, Europe’s largest open-air festival dedicated to traditional folk music, the pizzica, and the tarantella, takes place in Italy’s Puglia region.

Whether or not dancing works to sweat out a toxic venom, studies do show that dancing helps reduce stress and increases levels of serotonin, a hormone that helps regulate mood, sleep, and digestion.

“You know, whatever is biting at us, whether it’s grief or loss, we can move together, follow the rhythm of a drummer, and heal ourselves in a sense,” says Harsh. “The movement just takes over and we stop thinking about our troubles.”

Though if you do endure a lethal spider bite, we’d recommend the ER over two-stepping.

#4624. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4623. Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters said Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and shows,” according to Bloomberg.

Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”

Porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”

That’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

Also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

So the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

That’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

#4622. Creatures of Habit May Have Less Pain and Depression

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Creatures of habit—those who have a daily routine and stick to it—may benefit physically and psychologically from their predictable schedules, according to a new study published by researchers at the University of Missouri.

This might seem counterintuitive to people who live more unpredictable lives. Going about your day with no set schedule may seem exciting to some, but that chaos and uncertainty might be taking a hidden toll on well-being over time.

Temporarily escaping the confines of a routine during vacation is great, but living everyday life without the comfort of a set schedule creates anxiety and stress. Researchers also hypothesize that unstructured days can interfere with the body’s natural internal clock.

Circadian rhythms refer to the physical, mental, and behavioral changes we experience over a 24-hour cycle. Our body has an internal biological clock that has been honed by evolution over millions of years, largely calibrated to the lifestyle of a hunter-gatherer. Deviations from this ancient way of life often put us out of sync with our biological clock. Many psychologists believe this is an underappreciated source of unhappiness, fatigue, and illness.

When the sleep-wake cycle is disrupted, for example, it can have negative repercussions on other bodily systems. In other words, your body’s internal clock can impact your mood, hormones, energy level, cognitive abilities, metabolism, and more.

The primary driver of our sleep-wake cycle is light, but other factors influence it as well. Food, caffeine, exercise, stress, screen time, and more can potentially interfere with our natural internal clock. Scientists at the University of Missouri wanted to address whether maintaining a predictable daily routine helps keep our internal clock ticking the way it should.

The researchers recruited 67 subjects who were older adults—37 had insomnia, and 30 were good sleepers. Using surveys, the team examined whether regimented routines made a difference in health outcomes. Since the study included participants with insomnia, they could also determine whether insomnia played a role in any of the health outcomes reported.

The results revealed a striking difference between creatures of habit and those who lack structure in their daily lives. Participants who adhered to a daily routine reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression. This association was maintained in those who had insomnia.

While the study does not demonstrate causality, it suggests that regular mealtimes, wake-up times, social activities, and bedtimes furnish the brain with signals that help keep the internal clock functioning properly. In turn, this likely explains the better physical and psychological outcomes seen in those who live by set schedules.

The researchers conclude that sticking to a consistent routine is “associated with more favorable health outcomes and may represent a promising target for educational and interventional strategies for older adults, irrespective of insomnia status.”

The new findings support similar studies that found structured habits to be associated with lower mortality risks in aging seniors.

It happens to all of us—life’s events often disrupt our circadian rhythms every now and then. But there are evidence-based ways to get your internal clock back on track.

But sticking to a daily routine can help.

Another important factor is light management. As mentioned, light is the primary signal our brain uses to distinguish sleeping time from awake time. Bright lights in the morning, preferably sunlight, trigger your body to produce cortisol, the wakefulness hormone.

At night, darkness stimulates the release of the sleep hormone melatonin. Our use of artificial lights or screens at night can fool our brain into thinking that it is still daytime, hindering our ability to fall asleep. It is recommended to dim lights and stop screen usage 1-2 hours before bed.

Be mindful of alcohol, caffeine, and certain medications, as these agents can keep you awake or interfere with restful sleep.

Eating late at night, napping in the afternoon, and lack of physical activity can also make falling asleep difficult. Investing in a comfortable mattress and keeping your bedroom temperature cooler can also promote quality sleep.

See your doctor if you continue to experience trouble sleeping.

If you struggle with pain or depression, try adhering to consistent times for sleeping, eating, and other activities throughout your day. Adopting a predictable schedule is a natural and easy way to alleviate anxiety. Syncing your body's internal clock to the rhythms of the day promotes better mood, sleep, and overall health.

“Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults” by Eunjin Lee Tracy, et al. Journal of Behavioral Medicine, March 15, 2026.

#4621. Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), said in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

#4620. From Medical Marijuana to Marijuana Everywhere

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Walk through almost any American city, and you’ll likely smell marijuana smoke. Nonsmokers are complaining the most. Sidewalks. Hotels. Apartment buildings. Public spaces. Marijuana seems to be everywhere.

The modern medical marijuana movement gained momentum when patients with cancer, AIDS, and other serious illnesses sought relief. Compassion was a powerful argument for this group. So was criminal justice reform because sometimes penalties for possessing small amounts of marijuana were unreasonably high. But neither compassion nor decriminalization established that marijuana was effective for one illness, let alone dozens of diseases. Evidence supports certain cannabinoid-based treatments for rare indications, but not the safety or efficacy of cannabis dispensary products.

A systematic review by Petrilli and colleagues found higher-potency cannabis was associated with increased risks of psychosis and cannabis use disorder (CUD).

It started with the 1996 medical marijuana ballot measure in California, Proposition 215.

In 2012, Colorado and Washington became the first states to approve recreational marijuana legalization through statewide ballot initiatives.

Promises made to gain citizen support included fewer arrests, less illicit dealing, and medical benefits. There were also promises of tax revenue. Legalization also created retailers who need customers and investors expecting returns. Governments collect taxes and need money.

Kevin Sabet, PhD, and former Congressman Patrick Kennedy cofounded Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM) in 2013. They are advocates, but research has supported many of their policy suggestions.

One study analyzed 187,573 survey responses between 2018 and 2023. They raised questions about marketing practices, especially those reaching children. Xu and colleagues subsequently reported associations between cannabis advertising, price-based promotions, and initiation among adolescents and young adults.

Rotering and Apollonio also documented cannabis-industry lobbying concerning indoor smoking exemptions and pregnancy warnings.

Didn't we already learn these lessons from Big Tobacco?

Legal U.S. cannabis sales reached an estimated $29.1 billion in 2025, with industry projections anticipating further growth in 2026. But tax revenue isn’t the same as public health benefits.

Perhaps the most important finding about commercial cannabis is not how much is sold, but who’s buying it.

Cigarette manufacturers also depend on nicotine-dependent smokers. A disproportionate share of alcohol sales come from heavy drinkers. Fast-food and ultra-processed food companies benefit from frequent consumption. The marijuana industry is similar in this way. A study of Washington State's cannabis market estimated daily or near-daily consumers accounted for 91 percent of the market in 2016.

Reducing heavy cannabis consumption would reduce industry revenue and state tax receipts.

Approximately 62 percent of cannabis consumed in California during 2024 came from illicit sources.

The legal market expanded, but the illegal market remains as substantial as ever. Illegal cannabis products may be cheaper because producers and sellers avoid taxes, testing requirements, licensing fees, and other regulatory costs while offering anonymity and home or street delivery, providing a competitive advantage.

The marijuana smoked during the 1960s is not the cannabis sold in today's dispensaries. Historical estimates suggest marijuana in the 1960s often contained 1 percent THC or less. By the early 1990s, concentrations were around 3 percent, rising to approximately 4 percent in 1995. It did not stop there.

By 2014, average THC potency reached approximately 12 percent. By 2022, the DEA reported an average of 16 percent THC in monitored marijuana plants. Today's commercial flower may contain 20 to 30 percent THC, while concentrated products such as wax, shatter, and oils may contain 60 to 90 percent.

The dose escalation in potency over time is undeniable. No one today can say, as experts did in the ‘60s, that marijuana isn’t ever addicting, and today, addiction is more likely than ever.

Petrilli and colleagues' systematic review linked higher-potency cannabis with increased risks of psychosis and cannabis use disorder.

We didn’t legalize the marijuana of the '60s. We commercialized highly potent, concentrated forms of THC, without the long-term safety studies or FDA evidence expected of medicines.

But shouldn't people who never used cannabis receive protections comparable to those established for nonsmokers of tobacco? This is the most neglected question in cannabis public health, proving we are in a collective denial.

Secondhand smoke is firsthand smoke without consent.

Today, cigarette smoke is treated like poison, but cannabis smoke enters apartments, office buildings, hotel rooms, shared ventilation systems, and public spaces. Neighbors complain because they smell it. Sometimes they cannot escape it.

Cannabis smoke contains fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅), carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. The CDC warns secondhand cannabis smoke contains toxic and cancer-causing chemicals also present in tobacco smoke, sometimes at comparable or higher concentrations.

Cannabis does not contain nicotine, but cannabis smoke contains something tobacco smoke does not: THC. Controlled experiments in humans by Herrmann and colleagues demonstrated secondhand cannabis smoke exposure can produce measurable blood THC concentrations in poorly ventilated environments. They also reported secondhand exposure could produce subjective psychoactive effects.

Tripathi and colleagues studied 275 children and reported cannabis smoking inside the home was associated with approximately fivefold higher odds of evidence of cannabis in the body and brain by detecting urinary cannabinoid biomarkers. This doesn’t establish intoxication or addiction, but raises an obvious question: Why should children be exposed to THC-containing smoke?

Also, uncertainty about the magnitude of harm doesn’t prove repeated exposure is safe for children or adults.

Tobacco research taught homeowners, renters, hotel guests, and the rest of us another lesson: Smoke doesn’t disappear when the cigarette, joint, or bong goes out.

Tobacco researchers showed persistent residues in indoor environments. These alarming findings elevated concerns about infants' and young children's safety. Smoke-related combustion products remain on furniture, carpeting, clothing, walls, and household dust. Some residues can transfer or be resuspended. This is thirdhand smoke.

A 2025 JAMA Cardiology study by Mohammadi and colleagues reported associations between chronic marijuana smoking or THC-edible use (gummies, food including marijuana, such as the classic marijuana brownies) and impaired vascular endothelial function.

What about emergency department visits? Cannabis use disorder? Anhedonia? Psychosis? Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, characterized by recurrent episodes of severe nausea and vomiting? Asthma, impaired driving? Treatment costs? Costs may include addiction treatment, psychiatric and medical emergencies, the impacts of impaired driving, environmental exposure, and other health consequences.

We need prospective studies beginning before first cannabis use and continuing over time. We need to measure potential benefits and harms of legalization. We then need to use the FDA to establish medicinal benefit and calculate the risk-benefit balance.

Legalization, while circumventing science and the FDA, does not make marijuana safe. Slick marketing does not make it medicine. Nothing justifies exposing others to smoke.

The lessons of tobacco, alcohol, and cocaine should not be forgotten: Public health must come before commercial interests.

The next post in this series will examine the neuroscience of THC and the addiction, pregnancy, and prevention lessons we should already be applying.

#4619. Toyota and Subaru hit the ‘sweet spot’ with affordable electric SUVs

Toyota and Subaru’s new electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

Toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

After launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

Starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, said (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”

While she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

The Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average new vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a new vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

You can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

Subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante said the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

#4618. Why Men Ghost Their Therapists

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Counseling men is not like counseling women. If you try to counsel a man like a woman, it can quickly blow up—not with a bang, but a whimper. That male client may likely drop out. This is not to say that all men or all women are alike. It is to say that male gender-role socialization can shape what men need from counseling and how they engage with it.

This mismatch is understandable—women are the majority. More counselors, counseling clients, and counselor educators are women. Women made up 74.5 percent of the Bureau of Labor Statistics category “counselors, all other” in 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2026). Women made up 80.2 percent of students and 68.6 percent of full-time faculty in Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs-accredited counseling programs in 2024 (2025). Women were also more likely than men to receive counseling or therapy in 2024—16.9 percent compared with 10.9 percent (Briones and Villarroel, 2026).

Counseling is a female-dominated field, which is interesting because it was not always this way. Among faculty members in accredited counseling programs who earned their degrees in the 1960s and 1970s, only 26.7 percent were women. Five decades later, 63 percent were women (Baggerly and colleagues, 2017).

Men desperately need mental health support, but they are less likely than women to access counseling services (Briones and Villarroel, 2026). Yet, men die by suicide at nearly four times the rate of women (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026). Men also have higher drug-overdose death rates. In a federal analysis of deaths involving fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin, and oxycodone, the death rate was higher for men for every drug examined (Spencer and colleagues, 2023).

When men do attend counseling, many drop out. In a survey of 1,907 Australian men who had attended therapy, 44.8 percent reported dropping out. Among the men classified as dropouts, 26.6 percent attended only once and did not return. The most common reason was a lack of connection with the therapist (Seidler and colleagues, 2021).

Men need counseling, but they do not stay; a reason may be engagement. Men do not always engage with counseling when they enter services. This may happen because counselors assume male clients think, behave, and have treatment needs like female clients. But they do not always have the same needs.

Counselors get it wrong. They expect men to disclose emotionally vulnerable information at the outset of counseling. But vulnerable emotional disclosure can be difficult for men. Male gender-role socialization may not teach some men how to identify and express emotions, and it may associate vulnerable emotional disclosure with weakness. Specific messages associated with traditional masculinity, such as “no complaining,” “boys don’t cry,” and “pull yourself up by your bootstraps,” send the message to boys, who then become men, that they need to shut down their feelings, not share or open up about their struggles, and avoid seeking help (Levant and Parent, 2019; Seidler and colleagues, 2016).

For some men, the counseling office is unfamiliar and foreign. They feel like a fish out of water. If a counselor expects men to be vulnerable and disclose how they feel, the counselor may believe they are getting to the real issue. Yet the male client may experience it as being pushed into risky waters before rapport and safety have been built.

Counselors need to tread lightly. They should start the relationship in the safe zone, often at a more intellectual or practical level, until the man feels more comfortable and safety has been established. Counselors can ask what is happening, what needs to change, what the man has already tried, and what he wants from counseling.

This does not mean avoiding emotions or allowing the client to remain emotionally distant forever. It is a starting point. The focus is on pacing the work we do with men, where we progressively build up to emotional disclosure. A review of strategies for engaging men found support for collaborative, transparent, action-oriented, and goal-focused approaches. This also accounts for masculine socialization (Seidler and colleagues, 2018). Once the man feels that the counselor understands him and that the relationship is safe, they can move together into deeper, riskier waters.

Men need counseling. But getting men into counseling is only the first step. Counselors can also build strong connections that encourage clients to stay.

Baggerly, J., Tan, T. X., Pichotta, D., & Warner, A. (2017). Race, ethnicity, and gender of faculty members in APA- and CACREP-accredited programs: Changes over five decades. Journal of Multicultural Counseling and Development, 45(4), 292–303. https://doi.org/10.1002/jmcd.12079

Briones, E. M., & Villarroel, M. A. (2026). Mental health treatment among adults: United States, 2024. NCHS Data Brief, No. 564. National Center for Health Statistics.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (2026). Suicide data and statistics.

Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs. (2025). 2024 vital statistics report.

Levant, R. F., & Parent, M. C. (2019). The development and evaluation of a brief form of the Normative Male Alexithymia Scale (NMAS-BF). Journal of Counseling Psychology, 66(2), 224–233. https://doi.org/10.1037/cou0000312

Seidler, Z. E., Dawes, A. J., Rice, S. M., Oliffe, J. L., & Dhillon, H. M. (2016). The role of masculinity in men’s help-seeking for depression: A systematic review. Clinical Psychology Review, 49, 106–118. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2016.09.002

Seidler, Z. E., Rice, S. M., Ogrodniczuk, J. S., Oliffe, J. L., & Dhillon, H. M. (2018). Engaging men in psychological treatment: A scoping review. American Journal of Men’s Health, 12(6), 1882–1900. https://doi.org/10.1177/1557988318792157

#4617. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4616. Join NASA’s worldwide Voyager 1 celebration on Tuesday, November 17

Published Nov 10, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Back in 1998, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft became the farthest human-made object to ever travel beyond Earth. That technically means the intrepid explorer has been constantly breaking its own record for the last 28 years. But on November 18 (at 5:18 a.m. EST, to be exact), Voyager 1 will set a very specific and significant major record. At that point, it will officially be exactly one light-day away from its home planet. This means all future communications with the craft will take at least a full 24 hours to both send and receive.

It’s a monumental achievement for a piece of equipment originally intended to only survive only a few years in deep space, so why not celebrate the moment with NASA? The agency recently announced Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day, a worldwide event in which participants are encouraged to illuminate the night sky. Anytime after sunset on Tuesday, November 17, celebrants can aim either flashlight or smartphone towards the cosmos, then blink out the Morse signal “V-G-R,” NASA’s three-letter call sign. Don’t worry if you’re not necessarily versed in the code language, though. Simply blink along:

NASA even created a dedicated website to auto-flash the “VGR” Morse code, if that’s easier for beaming your dedication to the stars.

“A simple act. A shared moment. A celebration of humanity’s farthest reach,” NASA explained.

November 18 won’t be the end for Voyager 1, either. Thanks to recent equipment adjustments, NASA expects to squeeze at least a few more years’ of life from the spacecraft before it finally goes dark. At that point, Voyager 1 may become an inert piece of technology, but it will remain an interstellar monument to humanity’s curiosity and creativity.

#4615. 12 Features of the Experience of Addiction

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Do all addictions share one defining feature or characteristic? I tend to think not, and instead argue that addictions are better understood as having a family resemblance. Members of an extended family may not share one trait but rather a host of traits that overlap, crisscross, and connect the individuals. With addiction, there are patterns and weaves that connect the behaviors classified as addictions.

Here are 12 features or dimensions that I believe to be common characteristics of addiction.

Addiction is one way that a person can lose themselves. The loss can take multiple forms depending on the individual, the substance they use or behaviors in which they engage, and the contexts in which they live.

Addiction is a condition that imposes some limitations on people. Based on a wealth of data from my own experiences, I am certain that I cannot drink socially. I may be OK for a while, but I have good reason to believe that my drinking will pick up steam like a runaway locomotive. This certainty is bedrock for me and enables me to impose limitations on my own actions. I don’t go into bars even if you tell me that it’s a restaurant that serves drinks. I know a bar that sells food when I see it, and I am not going in it.

As I have gotten older and spent more time living in recovery, I’ve come to see that there is freedom within limitations. Too often we assume that having limitations imposes constraints that make us less free. This is true to some degree, but it obscures an important dimension of freedom.

Many philosophers would say that absolute freedom of choice is utterly terrifying; we humans would overload on the possibility and choice. I get overwhelmed trying to select a particular Triscuit cracker I want now that there are about 20 versions of that classic cracker. Getting overwhelmed by choices often leads to bad decisions.

A defining feature of addiction is that there are always negative consequences. This is a necessary condition. Addictions take time to develop. While early on, use may bring some benefit, at some point, the costs to a person become greater than the benefits.

Addiction is a multilevel condition with personal, interpersonal, and broader social dimensions. On the personal level, it is the person—not their brain—that is addicted. Within a person, it is a biochemical condition where drugs and certain behaviors affect functions of the brain but also different organs and systems.

Addiction is a full-bodied condition. My hangovers lasted days, often causing terrible nausea, shakes, and blurred vision among a host of physical ailments. When not drinking straight out of a bottle but out of a glass, my right hand always held the glass and swirled the contents around. I still catch myself doing that when served seltzer in a short glass. It brings me right back. The smell of beer turns my head while the smell of red wine turns my stomach. Our bodies hold memories and meanings.

There are important psychological dimensions to addiction as well. How we feel about ourselves and the beliefs we hold affect our use, which in turn affects how we regard ourselves. Addiction shapes our sense of self and how we see ourselves in the world.

For some, addiction is a spiritual condition, where drugs and behaviors try to fill a void or create meaning that seems to be missing.

Addiction is also a moral condition in which certain moral goods such as dignity, self-respect, care for our own selves and others, friendship, and flourishing are harmed. To claim addiction is a moral condition is not to claim it is a moral failure.

Addiction is also an interpersonal phenomenon. We humans are social creatures who are always in multiple relationships with family, friends, colleagues, neighbors, and other community members. Some of these are intentionally and freely chosen; others are a matter of circumstance or chance.

For many, the use of alcohol or other drugs made social interactions easier—at least at the beginning. Most of us learned how to use with others. We may have had drinking or using buddies, and many of our social interactions may have revolved around our use. When we progressed past a certain point, others may have cut us off, or we pruned people from our lives who questioned our use.

Addiction is a political phenomenon as well. By “political” I don’t mean electoral politics but the way that power flows through all the dimensions of our lives and communities. Power shapes the choices that some people face.

We are all free to quit paid employment, for example, but if we need to work to support ourselves or our families, or because we need insurance, we are free in theory rather than in practice. Also, we may feel compelled to adjust our careers or other significant life choices because of what others want for us or what society expects of us. Thus, we face all sorts of political or power pressures each day and try to make the best decisions possible.

Sometimes, we are caught between a rock and a hard place on the political level, and this may lead to unhealthy or bad decisions on both the personal and interpersonal levels.

In one sense, addiction is an equal opportunity condition; no one is immune to it. No one can be “addiction-proofed.”

In another sense, addiction is a very unequal opportunity condition. Some will have more social, economic, or educational protective layers that enable them to head off a problem before it gets really bad or to mitigate the bad consequences of their use. Others who lack these protective features and insulating layers may be subject to many more stressors and pay a much steeper price for their behaviors.

All of these dimensions—personal, interpersonal, and political—overlap and crisscross, creating a very dense fabric of tangled issues. This dense tangle can contribute to the development of an addiction.

#4614. Hyundai is shaking up its 2027 electric vehicle lineup: Here’s what’s changing

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the new IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai announced its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the new IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

The IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

It uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a new Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

The 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

On the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an update. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the new Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

#4613. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

#4612. Man with ‘demon face syndrome’ sees cat’s eyes in human faces

Published Nov 10, 2026 11:32 AM EST

Karl’s feline ordeal is detailed in a report published in the December 2026 issue of the journal Cortex. He has a form of palinopsia, a group of visual symptoms where an individual keeps seeing something even when it is not present. According to the Cleveland Clinic, palinopsia occurs when something disrupts vision-related processing in the brain. Many conditions and circumstances can cause it including migraine, seizures and epilepsy, strokes, some prescription drugs, and brain bleeds.

In Karl’s case, palinopsia leads to face distortions, a rare condition called prosopometamorphopsia (PMO), sometimes called  “demon face syndrome.” That scary nickname is because the distortions can sometimes look warped and scary like a demon.

Karl’s recurrent palinopsia began two years ago after part of Karl’s right temporal lobe was removed because the blood vessels between the arteries and veins there were tangled. This tangling can lead to a fatal brain bleed if left untreated. The right temporal lobe plays a critical role in face processing, so when Karl’s was partially removed it started messing with his ability to process faces.

“This case of Karl seeing his cat’s features in human faces and vice versa demonstrates that individual features can be pulled from memory and influence our ongoing perception,” Brad Duchaine, a study co-author at cognitive neurologist at Dartmouth College, said in a statement. Duchaine is also the principal investigator of the Social Perception Lab at Dartmouth, which studies these kinds of perception disorders.

After learning about Karl’s experience, Duchaine thought back to a 1986 study also published in Cortex. A woman on a bus saw a poodle on a passenger’s lap, and then saw that poodle’s face on every passenger riding the bus. The woman in that scenario had experienced a stroke nine months before.

However, in Karl’s situation, only components of faces are transferred rather than the entire face. To visually illustrate what Karl was experiencing, Duchaine prepared a sketch that he then fed into a large language model (LLM) to make the image look more realistic. He then shared the image with Karl, and the pair modified a set of images that are included in the report.

“AI provides researchers like us with the ability to generate more accurate visualizations of what people are experiencing when they’re having distorted visual perceptions,” Duchaine explained. “If you know what the person is experiencing, you can much better research what they’re dealing with and try to figure out ways to control it. And now the patient can also take part in that process of creating those visualizations.”

Duchaine’s lab has heard from over 250 people who experience face distortions like these, with some saying they have been told that they have a psychiatric problem. In a few of those cases, patients have been put on antipsychotics, when they are having visual problems, not a psychiatric issue.

The team plans to work with Karl in the future, to further probe when and if his condition changes over time and use similar AI tools to see what he is seeing. Understanding what he is seeing could help researchers better understand how to help people with this condition.

“The use of AI is also helpful for patients who want to convey not just to their healthcare professionals, but to their friends and family, what faces look like to them,” Duchaine concluded.

#4611. Use AI Last, Not First

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Most of us today do the same thing the moment a problem lands on our lap. Almost automatically, we open the chat window and pull up our favorite AI tool. Then we type in our prompt. Seconds later, a rather reasonable-appearing answer appears on the screen.

The problem isn’t that AI gives bad answers. It’s that AI seems like the easy way out. But it's deceptive, depriving us of the opportunity to use our human creative abilities to solve problems in new and novel ways.

AI cannot live in the now; it exists only as a snapshot of history and a crawl of data and the internet. That history cannot come up with ideas right now. And it turns out that right now is when you need the fresh ideas the most, to solve issues that are plaguing you. AI can only take a very narrow view of the past and try deceptively to apply it to the future.

So before you reach for AI first—because after all, AI is making everyone’s ideas the same anyhow—reach for it last. Here are some ideas for pushing back on the use of AI and instead relying on your own abilities to solve problems.

Instead of reaching for AI first, you go first. Write down three ideas that you have for the problem that just fell into your lap.

Write down the three worst ideas you can possibly come up with. Instead of pressing yourself to get it right from the get-go, stretch your solution mindset to think of issues creatively without the pressure to get it right.

Then take a stab at three ideas that will actually solve the problem. You may see some cross-pollination from the worst ideas list too.

In a recent MIT Media Lab experiment1, people who wrote down ideas first and then later switched to AI showed higher recall and activation. People who started with AI and then wrote on their own? They showed under-engagement.

Write down your ideas with a pen and paper first—old school. It turns out that doing it the old way may be more likely to make creativity and more lucid thinking2 happen for you.

I have friends in various industries who literally brag to me about the time they spend on their AI prompts. They say things like, “Nir—if you spend an extra five minutes on each prompt you put in, the AI answer is so much better.” I even have a friend who dedicates 15 minutes or more to each prompt. Every day.

Yet no matter how long you spend prompting the AI, you still get AI answers that sound much the same as the answers everyone else is getting. Instead, turn prompt time into being bored time.

Monitor the time you spend on AI each week asking it to do things for you. At the end of the week, see how much time you were on AI, and instead shift that time to being bored. So if it’s 20 minutes a week or 40 minutes a week, use that time differently. Plot down a 40-minute block of time during the week and call it “me time.” And then, instead of prompting an AI, be bored. Creativity and innovation will flow.

The research backs this. Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman3 found that experiencing a state of boredom increases creative potential, idea generation, and problem-solving performance.

So take the time you would waste on AI and invest it in yourself instead – the ideas you make while bored can be life-changing.

Chances are the problem that fell into your lap is rife with assumptions. Some of the assumptions are ones that you had made, some may be from a coworker, some may be from your ignorance of nuance, and some may just be stubborn histories.

Instead of getting bogged down with complexity, write the central problem on a piece of paper and then cross out all the assumptions made.

This process will bring clarity to an otherwise emotional or difficult problem by eliminating the assumptions that are preloaded into the problem. It also reframes the original problem in a simpler way, allowing you to solve it without all the extra fat and weight.

Technion professors Ronen, Goldschmidt, and Erez4 studied how people interpret a problem while solving it, which they call problem structuring. They found that extra clarity helped mainly because people used it to rethink the problem itself. How you frame the problem matters, not just the time you put in.

Overall, our urge to go to AI first for all our issues is a fallacy. We may think it's faster, cheaper, and better, but like all things that seem too good to be true, it is. If instead we try the three ideas listed above and then turn to AI as a last resort, we can begin to strengthen our creative problem-solving core to allow for new and novel ideas that no AI can ever generate.

1. Kosmyna, N., Hauptmann, E., Yuan, Y. T., Situ, J., Liao, X. H., Beresnitzky, A. V., ... & Maes, P. (2025). Your brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of cognitive debt when using an AI assistant for essay writing task. arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.08872, 4, 206.

2. Berninger, V. W. (2009). Highlights of programmatic, interdisciplinary research on writing. Learning disabilities research & practice, 24(2), 69-80.

3. Mann, S., & Cadman, R. (2014). Does being bored make us more creative?. Creativity Research Journal, 26(2), 165-173. https://doi.org/10.1080/10400419.2014.901073

#4610. Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

It’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its new Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, shows four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb

But the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

HMD took its first truck on November 2 and says it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler said Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”

The company ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

Owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

Tesla launched volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It says the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

So we’re left with proxies. Tesla says its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how big that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

The order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that shows whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

I think the semi is going to be a big seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

The 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

Good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

If you’re running an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs.
